content.caption: Enterprise-Grade Test Container Foundation
content.code:
# Enterprise Test Container with Multi-Stage Builds and Security

# Stage 1: Base image with security updates
FROM ubuntu:22.04 AS base

# Security: Non-root user and package updates
RUN groupadd -r testrunner && useradd -r -g testrunner testrunner \
    && apt-get update \
    && apt-get upgrade -y \
    && apt-get clean \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Stage 2: Dependencies installation
FROM base AS dependencies

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    curl \
    wget \
    gnupg \
    ca-certificates \
    software-properties-common \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Java (example for Java-based tests)
RUN mkdir -p /usr/share/man/man1 \
    && apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y openjdk-17-jdk-headless \
    && java -version \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Node.js (for JavaScript-based tests)
RUN curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_18.x | bash - \
    && apt-get install -y nodejs \
    && node --version \
    && npm --version

# Install Python (for Python-based tests)
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv \
    && python3 --version \
    && pip3 --version

# Stage 3: Browser installation
FROM dependencies AS browser

# Install Chrome for UI testing
RUN wget -q -O - https://dl-ssl.google.com/linux/linux_signing_key.pub | apt-key add - \
    && echo "deb http://dl.google.com/linux/chrome/deb/ stable main" >> /etc/apt/sources.list.d/google.list \
    && apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y google-chrome-stable \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Firefox for cross-browser testing
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y firefox \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Stage 4: Test framework installation
FROM browser AS frameworks

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency files
COPY package*.json ./  # Node.js
COPY requirements.txt ./  # Python
COPY pom.xml ./  # Java

# Install test frameworks and dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production \
    && pip3 install -r requirements.txt \
    && mvn dependency:go-offline -B

# Stage 5: Final optimized image
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Security: Non-root user
RUN groupadd -r testrunner && useradd -r -g testrunner testrunner \
    && apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y \
    curl \
    wget \
    openjdk-17-jdk-headless \
    nodejs \
    npm \
    python3 \
    python3-pip \
    google-chrome-stable \
    firefox \
    && apt-get clean \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy installed dependencies from frameworks stage
COPY --from=frameworks /app/node_modules /app/node_modules
COPY --from=frameworks /root/.m2 /root/.m2
COPY --from=frameworks /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages

# Copy test code
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .

# Set permissions
RUN chown -R testrunner:testrunner /app
USER testrunner

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1

# Test execution entry point
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/run-tests.sh"]

# Labels for metadata
LABEL maintainer="test-team@company.com" \
      version="1.0.0" \
      description="Test automation container with multi-language support" \
      test.frameworks="jest, pytest, junit" \
      test.browsers="chrome, firefox" \
      security.scan="true"

content.title: Container Foundation Principle
content.explanation:
Containers are about consistency, not virtualization.

While containers use OS-level virtualization, their primary value for testing is consistency. A container guarantees that what you test is exactly what gets deployed.

The magic of containers isn't in running isolated processes—it's in creating immutable, versioned, reproducible environments that eliminate the "it works on my machine" problem.

Build your test containers around the principle of reproducibility: every test run should start from exactly the same state, run in exactly the same environment, and produce exactly the same artifacts.

content.title: The Container Testing Pyramid
content.explanation:
Organizing tests in containerized environments:

• Layer 1: Unit Test Containers (Fast, Isolated)
  • Single-service containers
  • Mock external dependencies
  • Run in milliseconds
  • Goal: Test individual components in isolation
  
• Layer 2: Integration Test Containers (Service Interactions)
  • Multi-container setups with Docker Compose
  • Real service dependencies
  • Run in seconds to minutes
  • Goal: Test service interactions and APIs
  
• Layer 3: End-to-End Test Containers (Complete Systems)
  • Full application stacks
  • Real databases, caches, queues
  • Run in minutes
  • Goal: Test complete user journeys
  
• Layer 4: Performance Test Containers (Load & Stress)
  • Containerized load generators
  • Resource-limited application containers
  • Run in extended periods
  • Goal: Test system performance under load

In containerized testing:
• Each layer has appropriate container strategies
• Faster tests use simpler containers
• Complex tests use orchestrated containers
• All containers are versioned and reproducible

This pyramid ensures efficient resource usage and fast feedback.

content.title: Container Design Principles for Testing
content.explanation:
Effective test container design principles:

• Immutability: Containers should be immutable—changes create new containers
• Single Responsibility: Each container should have one clear purpose
• Ephemerality: Containers are disposable and stateless
• Declarative Configuration: Define containers as code (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml)
• Layered Architecture: Use multi-stage builds for optimization
• Security First: Run as non-root, minimal base images, regular updates
• Health Awareness: Include health checks for long-running containers
• Logging Ready: Configure logging for test execution monitoring
• Resource Conscious: Set appropriate resource limits
• Portable: Containers should run anywhere Docker is available

Design considerations for test containers:
• Size optimization for faster distribution
• Startup time optimization for rapid test execution
• Network configuration for inter-container communication
• Volume management for test data and results
• Environment variable configuration for test parameters

Well-designed containers are reliable, efficient, and maintainable.

content.title: Test Environment Strategy with Containers
content.explanation:
Managing test environments with containers:

• Environment Types:
  • Local Development: Docker on developer machines
  • CI Pipeline: Ephemeral containers per build
  • Integration Testing: Shared but isolated container networks
  • Staging/Pre-production: Production-like container orchestration
  • Performance Testing: Resource-limited container clusters

• Provisioning Strategies:
  • Docker Compose: For local and simple integration environments
  • Docker Swarm: For smaller-scale production-like environments
  • Kubernetes: For complex, scalable test environments
  • Nomad: For flexible workload orchestration

• Environment Management Patterns:
  • Ephemeral Environments: Created and destroyed per test run
  • Blue-Green Environments: Two identical environments for zero-downtime testing
  • Canary Environments: Gradual rollout for risk mitigation
  • Feature Branch Environments: Isolated environments per feature branch
  • Shared Pool Environments: Pool of environments for team usage

• Data Management:
  • Test Data Containers: Pre-populated data for testing
  • Database Snapshots: Volume snapshots for consistent starting points
  • Data Generation: On-the-fly test data generation
  • Data Cleanup: Automatic cleanup between test runs

Effective container environment strategy enables reliable, scalable testing.

content.title: Test Data Management in Containerized Environments
content.explanation:
Managing test data in containerized testing:

• Data Storage Strategies:
  • Volume Mounts: Persistent data across container restarts
  • Named Volumes: Managed Docker volumes for data isolation
  • Bind Mounts: Host directory mounts for development
  • tmpfs Mounts: In-memory storage for performance
  • Network Storage: NFS, Ceph, or cloud storage for distributed data

• Data Lifecycle Patterns:
  • Fresh Data Per Run: Generate new data for each test execution
  • Data Snapshots: Restore from snapshots for consistent starting points
  • Incremental Data: Build upon previous test data
  • Shared Data Pools: Centralized test data repositories

• Data Management Tools:
  • Database Migration Tools: Flyway, Liquibase for schema and data
  • Data Generation Tools: Faker, Factory Bot for synthetic data
  • Data Masking Tools: For production-like but anonymized data
  • Backup/Restore Tools: For database state management

• CI/CD Integration:
  • Data Setup in Pipeline: Scripted data preparation
  • Data Cleanup: Automatic cleanup after tests
  • Data Versioning: Version-controlled test data sets
  • Data Compliance: Ensure test data meets privacy regulations

Effective test data management prevents flaky tests and enables parallel execution.

content.title: Multi-Service Test Environment with Docker Compose
content.outcome: Complete isolated test environment in 2 minutes
content.prevention: Docker Compose with health checks and dependencies
content.details: Frontend Container (React app) → Backend API Container (Node.js) → User Service Container (Java) → Product Service Container (Python) → Database Container (PostgreSQL) → Cache Container (Redis) → Message Queue Container (RabbitMQ) → Test Runner Container (pytest + Selenium) → All connected via custom Docker network with DNS resolution

content.caption: Advanced Docker Compose for Microservice Testing
content.code:
# Complete Microservice Test Environment with Docker Compose
version: '3.8'

# Networks for isolation and communication
networks:
  test-network:
    driver: bridge
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
  monitoring-network:
    driver: bridge

# Volumes for persistent data
volumes:
  postgres-data:
    driver: local
  redis-data:
    driver: local
  test-results:
    driver: local
  test-data:
    driver: local

services:
  # Database
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: test-postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: testdb
      POSTGRES_USER: testuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
      POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS: "--encoding=UTF8 --locale=C"
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./sql/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
      - ./sql/test-data.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/test-data.sql
    networks:
      - test-network
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U testuser -d testdb"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 30s
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.5

  # Cache
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: test-redis
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes --requirepass redispass
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    networks:
      - test-network
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "redispass", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 256m
    cpus: 0.25

  # Message Queue
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3.11-management-alpine
    container_name: test-rabbitmq
    environment:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: rabbituser
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: rabbitpass
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_VHOST: /test
    ports:
      - "5672:5672"
      - "15672:15672"
    volumes:
      - ./rabbitmq/definitions.json:/etc/rabbitmq/definitions.json
      - ./rabbitmq/rabbitmq.conf:/etc/rabbitmq/rabbitmq.conf
    networks:
      - test-network
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "rabbitmq-diagnostics", "ping"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.5

  # User Service
  user-service:
    build:
      context: ./services/user-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
      args:
        BUILD_ENV: test
    container_name: test-user-service
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: testdb
      DB_USER: testuser
      DB_PASSWORD: testpass
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      REDIS_PORT: 6379
      REDIS_PASSWORD: redispass
      RABBITMQ_HOST: rabbitmq
      RABBITMQ_PORT: 5672
      NODE_ENV: test
      LOG_LEVEL: debug
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./services/user-service:/app
      - /app/node_modules
    networks:
      - test-network
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8080/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 40s
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 1g
    cpus: 1

  # Product Service
  product-service:
    build:
      context: ./services/product-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: test-product-service
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: testdb
      DB_USER: testuser
      DB_PASSWORD: testpass
      CACHE_HOST: redis
      CACHE_PORT: 6379
      CACHE_PASSWORD: redispass
      SERVICE_PORT: 8080
    ports:
      - "8082:8080"
    networks:
      - test-network
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8080/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.75

  # API Gateway
  api-gateway:
    image: nginx:1.23-alpine
    container_name: test-api-gateway
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/api-gateway.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf
      - ./nginx/test-upstream.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/upstream.conf
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    networks:
      - test-network
    depends_on:
      user-service:
        condition: service_healthy
      product-service:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8080/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 256m
    cpus: 0.25

  # Selenium Grid for UI Testing
  selenium-hub:
    image: selenium/hub:4.10.0
    container_name: selenium-hub
    ports:
      - "4442:4442"
      - "4443:4443"
      - "4444:4444"
    networks:
      - test-network
    environment:
      SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT: 4442
      SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT: 4443
      SE_JAVA_OPTS: -Xmx512m
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub/status"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 1g
    cpus: 1

  # Chrome nodes (scalable)
  selenium-chrome:
    image: selenium/node-chrome:4.10.0
    container_name: selenium-chrome-1
    shm_size: 2g
    depends_on:
      - selenium-hub
    environment:
      SE_EVENT_BUS_HOST: selenium-hub
      SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT: 4442
      SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT: 4443
      SE_NODE_MAX_SESSIONS: 4
      SE_NODE_OVERRIDE_MAX_SESSIONS: true
      SE_JAVA_OPTS: -Xmx512m
    networks:
      - test-network
    volumes:
      - /dev/shm:/dev/shm
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:5555/status"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 2g
    cpus: 1
    deploy:
      replicas: 2

  # Firefox nodes
  selenium-firefox:
    image: selenium/node-firefox:4.10.0
    container_name: selenium-firefox-1
    shm_size: 2g
    depends_on:
      - selenium-hub
    environment:
      SE_EVENT_BUS_HOST: selenium-hub
      SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT: 4442
      SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT: 4443
      SE_NODE_MAX_SESSIONS: 4
      SE_NODE_OVERRIDE_MAX_SESSIONS: true
    networks:
      - test-network
    volumes:
      - /dev/shm:/dev/shm
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:5555/status"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 2g
    cpus: 1

  # Test Runner
  test-runner:
    build:
      context: ./tests
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
      args:
        TEST_TYPE: e2e
    container_name: test-runner
    environment:
      API_BASE_URL: http://api-gateway:8080
      SELENIUM_HUB_URL: http://selenium-hub:4444
      DB_CONNECTION_STRING: postgresql://testuser:testpass@postgres:5432/testdb
      REDIS_URL: redis://:redispass@redis:6379
      RABBITMQ_URL: amqp://rabbituser:rabbitpass@rabbitmq:5672/test
      TEST_ENVIRONMENT: docker-compose
      PARALLEL_TESTS: 4
      TEST_TIMEOUT: 300
      LOG_LEVEL: INFO
    volumes:
      - test-results:/app/test-results
      - test-data:/app/test-data
      - ./tests:/app/tests
      - ./test-config:/app/config
    networks:
      - test-network
    depends_on:
      api-gateway:
        condition: service_healthy
      selenium-hub:
        condition: service_healthy
    command: ["./run-tests.sh", "--parallel", "--report", "html"]
    restart: "no"
    mem_limit: 2g
    cpus: 2

  # Monitoring
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.45.0
    container_name: test-prometheus
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"
    networks:
      - test-network
      - monitoring-network
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'
      - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus'
      - '--web.console.libraries=/etc/prometheus/console_libraries'
      - '--web.console.templates=/etc/prometheus/consoles'
      - '--storage.tsdb.retention.time=24h'
      - '--web.enable-lifecycle'
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.5

  # Grafana for visualization
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:10.0.0
    container_name: test-grafana
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
      - ./monitoring/grafana-dashboards:/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards
      - ./monitoring/grafana-datasources:/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    networks:
      - monitoring-network
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: admin
      GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS: grafana-piechart-panel
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.5

  # Test Report Server
  report-server:
    image: nginx:1.23-alpine
    container_name: test-report-server
    volumes:
      - test-results:/usr/share/nginx/html/test-results
      - ./nginx/report-server.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    ports:
      - "8085:80"
    networks:
      - test-network
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.1

content.title: Container Performance Optimization
content.explanation:
Optimizing container performance for testing:

• Image Optimization:
  • Multi-stage builds to minimize final image size
  • Layer caching to speed up builds
  • .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files
  • Alpine base images for smaller footprint
  • Combine RUN commands to reduce layers

• Runtime Optimization:
  • Appropriate resource limits (CPU, memory)
  • Shared memory (shm) configuration for browsers
  • Network optimization (custom bridges, MTU tuning)
  • Volume optimization (right storage driver)
  • Process management (init systems, signal handling)

• Startup Optimization:
  • Minimal entrypoint scripts
  • Lazy loading of heavy dependencies
  • Connection pooling for database connections
  • Warm-up scripts for JVM-based containers
  • Pre-pulled images in CI environments

• Test Execution Optimization:
  • Parallel container execution
  • Test distribution across containers
  • Intelligent test scheduling
  • Result aggregation and reporting
  • Artifact management optimization

Performance optimization techniques:
• Multi-stage builds reduce image size 70-90%
• Resource limits prevent resource exhaustion
• Parallel execution reduces test time 60-90%
• Layer caching reduces build time 50-80%
• Network optimization reduces latency 20-40%

Monitor container performance and optimize continuously.

content.title: Container Security for Testing
content.explanation:
Security considerations for test containers:

• Image Security:
  • Regular base image updates
  • Vulnerability scanning (Trivy, Clair, Grype)
  • Minimal base images
  • Signed images with content trust
  • Image provenance and attestation

• Runtime Security:
  • Non-root user execution
  • Read-only root filesystem
  • Security profiles (AppArmor, SELinux)
  • Seccomp profiles for system call filtering
  • Resource limits to prevent DoS
  • Network segmentation and firewalls

• Secrets Management:
  • Docker secrets for Swarm
  • Kubernetes secrets
  • HashiCorp Vault integration
  • Environment variable encryption
  • Temporary credentials with short TTL

• Compliance and Governance:
  • Image signing and verification
  • Audit logging of container activity
  • Compliance scanning (CIS benchmarks)
  • Policy enforcement (Open Policy Agent)
  • Regular security reviews

Security practices for test containers:
• Regular vulnerability scanning in CI/CD
• Principle of least privilege for container users
• Network segmentation for test environments
• Secrets rotation for test credentials
• Audit logging for compliance requirements

Secure containers protect both test data and infrastructure.

content.title: Branching Strategies and Container Testing
content.explanation:
Align container testing with branching strategies:

• Feature Branch Testing:
  • Isolated container environments per feature branch
  • Automated environment teardown
  • Resource tagging for cost management
  • Database per branch with schema isolation

• Trunk-Based Development:
  • Shared container registry with tagged images
  • Feature flags for incomplete features
  • Canary testing with container traffic splitting
  • Blue-green deployments with container orchestration

• Git Flow:
  • Different container tags for different branches
  • Release candidate containers
  • Hotfix containers with emergency patches
  • Long-lived container environments for release branches

• Environment Promotion:
  • Container images promoted through environments
  • Immutable containers from build to production
  • Configuration injection per environment
  • Database migration containers for schema changes

Container testing considerations:
• Image tagging strategy (git commit, branch, environment)
• Environment-specific configuration
• Test data management across branches
• Resource cleanup and reclamation
• Cost optimization for branch environments

Choose container testing strategy that supports your development workflow.

content.title: Container Strategy Principle
content.explanation:
Your container strategy should match your testing needs and infrastructure capabilities.

If you need fast, isolated unit tests, use simple single-container setups. If you need complex integration testing, use Docker Compose. If you need massive scale, use Kubernetes.

Design your containers to be composable: simple containers that can be combined into complex test environments. Each container should do one thing well and communicate clearly with other containers.

A good container strategy isn't just about running tests in containers—it's about designing test environments as code, versioning them alongside your tests, and creating reproducible, scalable testing infrastructure.

content.title: Kubernetes-Based Test Execution
content.explanation:
Running tests at scale with Kubernetes:

• Kubernetes Objects for Testing:
  • Pods: Ephemeral test execution units
  • Jobs: Run to completion for test suites
  • CronJobs: Scheduled test executions
  • Deployments: Long-running test services
  • Services: Network access to test components
  • ConfigMaps: Test configuration management
  • Secrets: Secure test credentials
  • PersistentVolumeClaims: Test data and results storage

• Test Execution Patterns:
  • Single Job: Complete test suite in one pod
  • Parallel Jobs: Multiple pods running tests in parallel
  • Work Queue: Central queue with worker pods
  • Fan-out/Fan-in: Distribute tests, aggregate results
  • Sidecar Pattern: Test runner with supporting containers

• Scaling Strategies:
  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaling: Scale based on test queue length
  • Cluster Autoscaling: Add nodes for peak test loads
  • Resource-based Scheduling: Schedule tests based on resource requirements
  • Affinity/Anti-affinity: Control pod distribution across nodes

• Benefits:
  • Massive parallel test execution
  • Self-healing test infrastructure
  • Resource efficiency through bin packing
  • Declarative test environment management
  • Integration with production deployment patterns

Kubernetes enables enterprise-scale test automation.

content.title: Service Mesh Testing
content.explanation:
Testing in service mesh environments:

• Service Mesh Components:
  • Data Plane: Proxies (Envoy) handling traffic
  • Control Plane: Management (Istio, Linkerd, Consul)
  • Service Discovery: Automatic service registration
  • Traffic Management: Load balancing, routing, splitting
  • Observability: Metrics, logs, traces
  • Security: mTLS, authentication, authorization

• Testing Strategies:
  • Traffic Splitting: Canary testing with Istio
  • Fault Injection: Test failure scenarios
  • Circuit Breaker Testing: Validate resilience patterns
  • Security Testing: mTLS configuration and policies
  • Performance Testing: Mesh overhead measurement
  • Migration Testing: Service-to-service mesh migration

• Test Tools:
  • Istio: For Kubernetes-based service mesh
  • K6 with xk6-distributed-sampling: Load testing with mesh integration
  • Toxiproxy: Failure injection
  • Fortio: Load testing and mesh validation
  • Service Mesh Performance: Benchmarking tools

• Testing Considerations:
  • Mesh configuration validation
  • Proxy resource usage
  • Latency impact measurement
  • Security policy verification
  • Multi-cluster mesh testing

Service mesh testing ensures reliability in microservices architectures.

content.title: Distributed Test Execution
content.explanation:
Running tests across distributed container clusters:

• Distribution Patterns:
  • Test Sharding: Split test suite across containers
  • Data Parallelism: Same tests with different data
  • Geographic Distribution: Tests from different regions
  • Cloud Bursting: Scale to cloud during peak loads
  • Hybrid Execution: Mix of local and cloud containers

• Coordination Mechanisms:
  • Message Queues: RabbitMQ, Kafka for test coordination
  • Distributed Locks: Redis, etcd for resource coordination
  • Work Queues: Celery, Apache Airflow for task management
  • Service Discovery: Consul, etcd for service location
  • Distributed Tracing: Jaeger, Zipkin for test flow analysis

• Result Aggregation:
  • Centralized Storage: Object storage for test results
  • Distributed Databases: Cassandra, CockroachDB for results
  • Search Engines: Elasticsearch for test result analysis
  • Real-time Dashboards: Streaming results to dashboards
  • Alerting Systems: Notifications for test failures

• Challenges:
  • Network latency between containers
  • Data consistency across distributed tests
  • Result aggregation and correlation
  • Resource management and optimization
  • Cost control for cloud resources

Distributed testing enables massive scale but requires careful coordination.

content.title: Chaos Engineering in Containerized Environments
content.explanation:
Testing resilience with chaos engineering:

• Chaos Principles:
  • Hypothesis-Driven: Start with a hypothesis about system behavior
  • Blast Radius Control: Limit impact of chaos experiments
  • Observability: Measure system response to chaos
  • Automation: Automate chaos experiments
  • Safety: Ability to abort experiments quickly

• Chaos Tools for Containers:
  • Chaos Mesh: Kubernetes-native chaos engineering
  • Litmus: Chaos engineering for cloud-native
  • PowerfulSeal: Kubernetes chaos engineering
  • Chaos Toolkit: Vendor-neutral chaos engineering
  • Gremlin: Enterprise chaos engineering platform

• Chaos Experiments:
  • Pod Failure: Kill pods randomly or selectively
  • Network Chaos: Introduce latency, packet loss, partition
  • Resource Stress: CPU, memory, disk pressure
  • Time Chaos: Clock skew, time travel
  • Cloud Chaos: Simulate cloud provider failures

• Testing Integration:
  • Pre-chaos baseline tests
  • During-chaos resilience tests
  • Post-chaos recovery tests
  • Automated chaos in CI/CD pipelines
  • Canary testing with chaos injection

Chaos engineering builds confidence in system resilience.

content.caption: Enterprise Kubernetes Test Execution Framework
content.code:
# Enterprise-Grade Kubernetes Test Execution Configuration

# Test Namespace Configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-execution
  labels:
    environment: test
    purpose: test-automation
---

# Test Configuration ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: test-config
  namespace: test-execution
data:
  test-suites.yaml: |
    suites:
      unit:
        image: registry.company.com/tests/unit:latest
        command: ["npm", "test", "--", "--testPathPattern=.*\.test\.js$"]
        timeout: 300
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 250m
            memory: 512Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 1Gi
      integration:
        image: registry.company.com/tests/integration:latest
        command: ["pytest", "tests/integration/", "-v"]
        timeout: 600
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 1Gi
          limits:
            cpu: 1000m
            memory: 2Gi
      e2e:
        image: registry.company.com/tests/e2e:latest
        command: ["./run-e2e.sh", "--parallel", "4"]
        timeout: 1800
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 1000m
            memory: 2Gi
          limits:
            cpu: 2000m
            memory: 4Gi
  test-env.yaml: |
    environment:
      LOG_LEVEL: INFO
      TEST_REPORT_DIR: /test-results
      TEST_DATA_DIR: /test-data
      PARALLEL_EXECUTION: "true"
      MAX_RETRIES: 3
    services:
      database:
        host: test-postgres.test-execution.svc.cluster.local
        port: 5432
        database: testdb
      redis:
        host: test-redis.test-execution.svc.cluster.local
        port: 6379
      api:
        host: api-service.test-execution.svc.cluster.local
        port: 8080
---

# Test Secrets
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test-secrets
  namespace: test-execution
type: Opaque
data:
  db-password: dGVzdHBhc3M=  # testpass
  api-key: YXBpLWtleS1zZWNyZXQ=  # api-key-secret
  redis-password: cmVkaXNwYXNz  # redispass
---

# Test Results Volume
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: test-results-pvc
  namespace: test-execution
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
---

# Unit Test Job
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: unit-tests
  namespace: test-execution
  labels:
    test-type: unit
    component: test-automation
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400  # Clean up after 24 hours
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        test-type: unit
        component: test-automation
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: unit-test-runner
        image: registry.company.com/tests/unit:latest
        command: ["npm", "test", "--", "--testPathPattern=.*\.test\.js$"]
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: "test"
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: test-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: test-config
            optional: true
        - secretRef:
            name: test-secrets
            optional: true
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 250m
            memory: 512Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 1Gi
        volumeMounts:
        - name: test-results
          mountPath: /test-results
        - name: test-data
          mountPath: /test-data
        - name: test-config-volume
          mountPath: /etc/test-config
          readOnly: true
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["test", "-f", "/test-results/.running"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["test", "-f", "/test-results/.ready"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
      volumes:
      - name: test-results
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: test-results-pvc
      - name: test-data
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: test-config-volume
        configMap:
          name: test-config
          items:
          - key: test-env.yaml
            path: test-env.yaml
          - key: test-suites.yaml
            path: test-suites.yaml
---

# Parallel Integration Test Job
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: integration-tests-parallel
  namespace: test-execution
spec:
  completions: 4  # Number of pods to run
  parallelism: 4  # Number of pods to run in parallel
  completions: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        test-type: integration
        test-execution: parallel
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: integration-test-worker
        image: registry.company.com/tests/integration:latest
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          # Get worker index from downward API
          WORKER_INDEX=$JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX
          TOTAL_WORKERS=4
          
          # Calculate test distribution
          TEST_FILES=$(find tests/integration -name "*.py" | sort)
          TOTAL_TESTS=$(echo "$TEST_FILES" | wc -l)
          TESTS_PER_WORKER=$((TOTAL_TESTS / TOTAL_WORKERS))
          REMAINDER=$((TOTAL_TESTS % TOTAL_WORKERS))
          
          # Calculate start and end indices
          START=$((WORKER_INDEX * TESTS_PER_WORKER))
          if [ $WORKER_INDEX -lt $REMAINDER ]; then
            START=$((START + WORKER_INDEX))
            END=$((START + TESTS_PER_WORKER + 1))
          else
            START=$((START + REMAINDER))
            END=$((START + TESTS_PER_WORKER))
          fi
          
          # Run assigned tests
          echo "Worker $WORKER_INDEX running tests $START to $END"
          TEST_FILES_ARRAY=($TEST_FILES)
          SELECTED_TESTS="${TEST_FILES_ARRAY[@]:$START:$((END-START))}"
          
          pytest $SELECTED_TESTS -v --junitxml=/test-results/worker-$WORKER_INDEX.xml
        env:
        - name: JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.annotations['batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index']
        - name: WORKER_COUNT
          value: "4"
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 1Gi
          limits:
            cpu: 1000m
            memory: 2Gi
        volumeMounts:
        - name: test-results
          mountPath: /test-results
        - name: shared-data
          mountPath: /shared-data
      volumes:
      - name: test-results
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: test-results-pvc
      - name: shared-data
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
          sizeLimit: 1Gi
---

# Test Result Aggregator
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-result-aggregator
  namespace: test-execution
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-result-aggregator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-result-aggregator
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: aggregator
        image: registry.company.com/tools/result-aggregator:latest
        command: ["python", "aggregate_results.py"]
        args: ["--input-dir", "/test-results", "--output-dir", "/aggregated-results"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: test-results
          mountPath: /test-results
          readOnly: true
        - name: aggregated-results
          mountPath: /aggregated-results
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 256Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 200m
            memory: 512Mi
      volumes:
      - name: test-results
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: test-results-pvc
      - name: aggregated-results
        emptyDir: {}
---

# Test Report Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test-report-service
  namespace: test-execution
spec:
  selector:
    app: test-result-aggregator
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
---

# Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for Test Workers
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: test-worker-autoscaler
  namespace: test-execution
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: test-worker-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 60
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 60
---

# Test Execution Monitoring
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: test-execution-monitor
  namespace: test-execution
  labels:
    release: prometheus
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      component: test-automation
  endpoints:
  - port: metrics
    interval: 30s
    scrapeTimeout: 10s
    path: /metrics
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
    - test-execution

content.title: Multi-Architecture Container Testing

Testing across different hardware architectures:

• Architecture Considerations:
  • x86_64 (amd64): Traditional Intel/AMD servers and desktops
  • ARM64 (aarch64): Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton, Raspberry Pi
  • ARMv7: Older ARM devices
  • s390x: IBM mainframes
  • ppc64le: IBM Power systems

• Multi-Arch Strategies:
  • Buildx: Docker Buildx for multi-platform builds
  • Manifest Lists: Single tag pointing to multiple architecture images
  • Emulation: QEMU for cross-architecture execution
  • Native Builders: Build on actual architecture hardware
  • Cloud Builders: Cloud services for multi-arch builds

• Testing Approaches:
  • Architecture-Specific Test Suites
  • Cross-Architecture Compatibility Testing
  • Performance Comparison Across Architectures
  • Library and Dependency Compatibility
  • Endianness and Alignment Testing

• CI/CD Integration:
  • Multi-arch builds in pipelines
  • Architecture-specific test execution
  • Performance benchmarking across architectures
  • Compatibility test automation
  • Release validation for all supported architectures

Multi-architecture testing ensures software works everywhere.

content.title: GitOps for Test Environments
content.explanation:
Managing test environments with GitOps:

• GitOps Principles:
  • Declarative: Desired state declared in Git
  • Versioned: All changes version controlled
  • Automated: Automated synchronization to desired state
  • Audited: All changes tracked and auditable
  • Continuous: Continuous reconciliation to desired state

• GitOps Tools:
  • ArgoCD: Declarative GitOps for Kubernetes
  • FluxCD: GitOps operator for Kubernetes
  • Jenkins X: GitOps native CI/CD
  • Tekton: Cloud-native CI/CD with GitOps

• Test Environment Management:
  • Environment definitions in Git
  • Automated environment provisioning
  • Self-service test environments
  • Environment promotion through Git
  • Automated cleanup and reclamation

• Benefits for Testing:
  • Reproducible test environments
  • Version-controlled environment configurations
  • Automated environment updates
  • Collaboration through pull requests
  • Audit trail for compliance

GitOps brings DevOps best practices to test environment management.

content.title: Test Container Metrics and Monitoring
content.explanation:
Monitoring containerized test execution:

• Key Metrics:
  • Container Metrics: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network
  • Test Execution Metrics: Pass/fail rates, execution time, flakiness
  • Resource Utilization: Efficiency of test resource usage
  • Pipeline Metrics: Build times, image sizes, push/pull times

  • Security vulnerability detection

• Dashboard Design:
  • Test execution overview

  • Test performance trends

Good monitoring turns test execution data into actionable insights.

content.title: Container Testing Principle
content.explanation:
Containers should make testing better, not just different.

The goal of containerized testing isn't to use containers—it's to achieve faster, more reliable, and more scalable testing. Every container decision should serve that goal.

Good containerized testing:
• Reduces environment-related failures
• Speeds up test execution through parallelization
• Makes tests more reliable through isolation
• Scales with your testing needs
• Integrates seamlessly with your development workflow

Don't containerize for the sake of containerization. Containerize to solve real testing problems and enable better software delivery.

The best container strategy is the one that makes testing so reliable and fast that it becomes invisible—just a natural part of delivering quality software.

content.title: Why Infrastructure Testing is Critical
content.explanation: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) brings software engineering practices to infrastructure management, but without proper testing, it can lead to costly outages, security breaches, and compliance violations. Traditional infrastructure changes were manual and slow; IaC enables rapid changes that require automated validation. Infrastructure testing ensures that your cloud resources are provisioned correctly, securely, and in compliance with organizational policies. Without testing, you risk configuration drift, security vulnerabilities, and production failures.

content.title: Terraform Testing Strategy
content.explanation: Terraform testing requires a multi-layered approach. Start with static analysis using tools like TFLint and Checkov to catch syntax errors and security issues. Implement unit tests for individual modules using Terratest or custom Go tests to validate resource configurations. Create integration tests that deploy complete stacks and validate end-to-end functionality. Finally, implement compliance tests using Open Policy Agent (OPA) to enforce organizational policies. This layered strategy ensures comprehensive coverage from code quality to production readiness.

content.title: Security Scanning Tools for IaC
content.explanation: Security scanning tools analyze IaC configurations for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compliance violations before deployment. Checkov scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, and other IaC formats for security issues using a library of 1000+ policies. TFLint validates Terraform code for best practices and potential errors. tfsec focuses specifically on Terraform security. These tools integrate into CI/CD pipelines to provide shift-left security, catching issues early in the development process. They can be customized with organizational policies and integrated with security information and event management (SIEM) systems.

content.caption: GitHub Actions Pipeline for Terraform Testing
content.code:
name: Terraform Testing Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
    paths:
      - 'terraform/**'
      - '.github/workflows/terraform-testing.yml'
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
    paths:
      - 'terraform/**'

env:
  TERRAFORM_VERSION: '1.5.0'
  AWS_REGION: 'us-east-1'
  TF_WORKSPACE: 'test'

jobs:
  # Job 1: Static Analysis and Security Scanning
  static-analysis:
    name: 'Static Analysis & Security'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
    
    - name: Setup Terraform
      uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      with:
        terraform_version: ${{ env.TERRAFORM_VERSION }}
    
    - name: Terraform fmt
      id: fmt
      run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
    
    - name: Terraform validate
      id: validate
      run: terraform validate
    
    - name: Run TFLint
      id: tflint
      uses: terraform-linters/setup-tflint@v3
      with:
        tflint_version: 'latest'
    
    - name: Run Checkov security scan
      id: checkov
      uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@master
      with:
        directory: ./terraform
        framework: terraform
        quiet: true
      continue-on-error: true
    
    - name: Upload security reports
      if: always()
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: security-reports
        path: |
          checkov-report.json
          tflint-report.json
  
  # Job 2: Plan Generation and Review
  terraform-plan:
    name: 'Terraform Plan'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: static-analysis
    
    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
    
    - name: Setup Terraform
      uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      with:
        terraform_version: ${{ env.TERRAFORM_VERSION }}
    
    - name: Configure AWS credentials
      uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v2
      with:
        aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
        aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}
    
    - name: Terraform Init
      run: terraform init -backend=false
    
    - name: Generate Terraform Plan
      id: plan
      run: |
        terraform plan -out=tfplan.binary
        terraform show -json tfplan.binary > tfplan.json
    
    - name: Analyze Plan for Destructive Changes
      id: analyze-plan
      run: |
        # Custom script to check for destructive changes
        python scripts/analyze_terraform_plan.py tfplan.json
        
        if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
          echo "Destructive changes detected!"
          exit 1
        fi
    
    - name: Upload Terraform Plan
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: terraform-plan
        path: tfplan.json
  
  # Job 3: Integration Testing with Terratest
  integration-tests:
    name: 'Integration Tests'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: terraform-plan
    
    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
    
    - name: Setup Go
      uses: actions/setup-go@v4
      with:
        go-version: '1.20'
    
    - name: Run Terratest Integration Tests
      id: terratest
      run: |
        cd tests/integration
        go test -v -timeout 30m
      env:
        AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
        AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        AWS_REGION: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}
        TF_VAR_environment: 'test'
        TF_VAR_test_mode: 'true'
    
    - name: Upload Test Results
      if: always()
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: integration-test-results
        path: tests/integration/test-results/
  
  # Job 4: Compliance Testing
  compliance-testing:
    name: 'Compliance Testing'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: terraform-plan
    
    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
    
    - name: Run Open Policy Agent (OPA) Tests
      id: opa
      uses: open-policy-agent/setup-opa@v2
      with:
        version: 'latest'
    
    - name: Evaluate OPA Policies
      run: |
        # Load Terraform plan
        PLAN=$(cat tfplan.json)
        
        # Evaluate against OPA policies
        opa eval --data policies/ --input tfplan.json \
          "data.terraform.analysis"
        
        # Check for policy violations
        if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
          echo "Policy violations detected!"
          exit 1
        fi
    
    - name: Upload Compliance Reports
      if: always()
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: compliance-reports
        path: compliance-report.json

content.title: Policy as Code with Open Policy Agent
content.explanation: Open Policy Agent (OPA) enables policy as code, allowing you to define and enforce organizational policies across your infrastructure. Unlike traditional compliance tools, OPA uses a declarative language called Rego to express policies as code. Policies can validate Terraform plans, Kubernetes manifests, API requests, and other configurations. OPA integrates with CI/CD pipelines to provide automated policy enforcement, preventing non-compliant infrastructure from being deployed. Policies can cover security requirements, cost controls, naming conventions, tagging standards, and regulatory compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS).

content.caption: OPA Policies for Infrastructure Compliance
content.code:
# policies/terraform/security.rego
package terraform.security

# Deny S3 buckets without encryption
default allow_s3_bucket = false

allow_s3_bucket {
    # Check if bucket has server-side encryption
    bucket := input.resource_changes[_]
    bucket.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
    bucket.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration != null
}

violation[msg] {
    bucket := input.resource_changes[_]
    bucket.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
    not bucket.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration
    msg := sprintf("S3 bucket %s must have server-side encryption enabled", [bucket.name])
}

# policies/terraform/cost.rego
package terraform.cost

# Require cost allocation tags on all resources
default require_cost_tags = false

require_cost_tags {
    resource := input.resource_changes[_]
    # Skip data sources and meta resources
    not startswith(resource.type, "data")
    not startswith(resource.type, "terraform")
    
    # Check for required tags
    required_tags := {"Environment", "Owner", "CostCenter"}
    present_tags := {t | resource.change.after.tags[t]}
    missing_tags := required_tags - present_tags
    count(missing_tags) == 0
}

violation[msg] {
    resource := input.resource_changes[_]
    not startswith(resource.type, "data")
    not startswith(resource.type, "terraform")
    
    required_tags := {"Environment", "Owner", "CostCenter"}
    present_tags := {t | resource.change.after.tags[t]}
    missing_tags := required_tags - present_tags
    count(missing_tags) > 0
    
    msg := sprintf("Resource %s missing required tags: %v", [resource.address, missing_tags])
}

# policies/terraform/security_groups.rego
package terraform.security_groups

# Deny security groups with overly permissive rules
default allow_security_group = true

allow_security_group = false {
    sg := input.resource_changes[_]
    sg.type == "aws_security_group"
    
    # Check for overly permissive ingress rules
    rule := sg.change.after.ingress[_]
    rule.cidr_blocks[_] == "0.0.0.0/0"
    rule.from_port == 22  # SSH open to world
}

violation[msg] {
    sg := input.resource_changes[_]
    sg.type == "aws_security_group"
    
    rule := sg.change.after.ingress[_]
    rule.cidr_blocks[_] == "0.0.0.0/0"
    rule.from_port == 22
    
    msg := sprintf("Security group %s has SSH (port 22) open to the world", [sg.name])
}

# policies/terraform/size_limits.rego
package terraform.size_limits

# Enforce instance size limits based on environment
default allow_instance_size = true

allow_instance_size = false {
    instance := input.resource_changes[_]
    instance.type == "aws_instance"
    
    # Get environment from tags
    env := instance.change.after.tags.Environment
    size := instance.change.after.instance_type
    
    # Define size limits per environment
    env == "dev"
    not re_match("^t3\.(micro|small|medium)$", size)
}

violation[msg] {
    instance := input.resource_changes[_]
    instance.type == "aws_instance"
    
    env := instance.change.after.tags.Environment
    size := instance.change.after.instance_type
    
    env == "dev"
    not re_match("^t3\.(micro|small|medium)$", size)
    
    msg := sprintf("Development instance %s size %s exceeds limit (max t3.medium)", [instance.name, size])
}

content.title: Infrastructure Integration Testing
content.explanation: Infrastructure integration testing validates that complete infrastructure stacks work together correctly. Unlike unit tests that validate individual components, integration tests deploy entire environments and validate end-to-end functionality. Terratest is a popular Go library for writing infrastructure integration tests. Tests typically follow this pattern: 1) Deploy infrastructure using Terraform, 2) Validate resource creation and configuration, 3) Test application functionality on the infrastructure, 4) Clean up resources. Integration tests should run in isolated environments (separate AWS accounts or resource groups) to prevent interference with other tests or production.

content.title: What is GitOps Testing?
content.explanation: GitOps testing validates that Git-based deployment workflows operate correctly, safely, and efficiently. Unlike traditional deployment testing, GitOps testing focuses on the synchronization between Git repositories and live infrastructure, configuration validation, automated rollback testing, and continuous compliance verification. GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications, with automated tools (like Argo CD or Flux) synchronizing the live state with the desired state in Git. Testing ensures this synchronization works correctly, configurations are valid, and deployments are reliable.

content.title: GitOps Testing Pillars
rows: Argo CD/Flux health checks, custom validators
Sync speed, resource utilization, scale testing

steps.title: Repository Structure Design
steps.description: Organize Git repositories for GitOps workflows.
steps.details: Create separate directories for environments (dev, staging, prod). Use Git branches or separate repos for different environments. Implement Kustomize or Helm for environment-specific overrides.

steps.title: Post-sync Validation

steps.details: Create post-sync hooks or CI/CD jobs that run integration tests, smoke tests, and health checks after deployments.

steps.title: Drift Detection Setup

steps.details: Monitor sync status, deployment frequency, error rates, and resource health. Configure alerts for sync failures, drift detection, and performance issues.

content.title: Validating Kubernetes Manifests
content.explanation: Kubernetes manifest validation is critical for GitOps because invalid YAML can break entire deployment pipelines. Validation includes syntax checking, schema validation, security scanning, and best practice enforcement. Tools like kubeval validate manifests against the Kubernetes API schema, ensuring compatibility with your cluster version. Conftest uses Open Policy Agent (OPA) to enforce custom policies for security, compliance, and organizational standards. Kube-score evaluates manifests against security and reliability best practices. These validations should run in CI/CD pipelines before manifests are committed to Git, preventing broken configurations from reaching production.

content.caption: GitHub Actions Pipeline for Kubernetes Validation
content.code:
name: Kubernetes Manifest Validation

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
    paths:
      - 'kubernetes/**'
      - 'manifests/**'
      - '.github/workflows/k8s-validation.yml'

jobs:
  validate-manifests:
    name: 'Validate Kubernetes Manifests'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
      with:
        fetch-depth: 0
    
    - name: Setup Kubernetes tools
      run: |
        # Install kubeval for schema validation
        curl -LO https://github.com/instrumenta/kubeval/releases/latest/download/kubeval-linux-amd64.tar.gz
        tar xf kubeval-linux-amd64.tar.gz
        sudo mv kubeval /usr/local/bin/
        
        # Install kube-score for best practices
        curl -L https://github.com/zegl/kube-score/releases/download/v1.16.1/kube-score_1.16.1_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
        sudo mv kube-score /usr/local/bin/
        
        # Install conftest for policy validation
        curl -L https://github.com/open-policy-agent/conftest/releases/download/v0.44.0/conftest_0.44.0_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz | tar xz
        sudo mv conftest /usr/local/bin/
    
    - name: Find all Kubernetes manifests
      id: find-manifests
      run: |
        find . -type f \( -name "*.yaml" -o -name "*.yml" \) \
          -path "./kubernetes/*" -o \
          -path "./manifests/*" -o \
          -path "./deployments/*" | \
          grep -v node_modules | \
          grep -v .git > manifests.txt
        
        echo "Found $(wc -l < manifests.txt) manifests"
        cat manifests.txt
    
    - name: Validate with kubeval
      id: kubeval
      run: |
        while read manifest; do
          echo "Validating $manifest with kubeval..."
          kubeval --strict $manifest \
            --kubernetes-version 1.27 \
            --schema-location https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yannh/kubernetes-json-schema/master \
            || exit 1
        done < manifests.txt
    
    - name: Check best practices with kube-score
      id: kube-score
      run: |
        while read manifest; do
          echo "Scoring $manifest with kube-score..."
          kube-score score $manifest --output-format ci \
            || echo "kube-score warnings/errors found (continuing)"
        done < manifests.txt
    
    - name: Validate policies with conftest
      id: conftest
      run: |
        # Run conftest against all manifests
        conftest test --policy policies/kubernetes/ manifests.txt
      continue-on-error: false
    
    - name: Security scan with Checkov
      id: checkov
      uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@master
      with:
        directory: .
        framework: kubernetes
        quiet: true
        skip_check: CKV_K8S_2,CKV_K8S_6  # Skip specific checks if needed
      continue-on-error: true
    
    - name: Upload validation reports
      if: always()
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: k8s-validation-reports
        path: |
          checkov-report.json
          kubeval-report.json
    
    - name: Comment on PR with results
      if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
      uses: actions/github-script@v6
      with:
        script: |
          const results = {
            kubeval: '${{ steps.kubeval.outcome }}',
            kubeScore: '${{ steps.kube-score.outcome }}',
            conftest: '${{ steps.conftest.outcome }}',
            checkov: '${{ steps.checkov.outcome }}'
          };
          
          const success = Object.values(results).every(r => r === 'success');
          
          let message = `## Kubernetes Validation Results\n`;
          message += `✅ **kubeval**: ${results.kubeval === 'success' ? 'Passed' : 'Failed'}\n`;
          message += `📊 **kube-score**: ${results.kubeScore === 'success' ? 'Passed' : 'Warnings'}\n`;
          message += `🔒 **conftest**: ${results.conftest === 'success' ? 'Passed' : 'Failed'}\n`;
          message += `🛡️ **Checkov**: ${results.checkov === 'success' ? 'Passed' : 'Warnings'}\n`;
          
          if (success) {
            message += `\n✅ **All validations passed! Ready to merge.**`;
          } else {
            message += `\n❌ **Some validations failed. Please review the logs.**`;
          }
          
          github.rest.issues.createComment({
            issue_number: context.issue.number,
            owner: context.repo.owner,
            repo: context.repo.repo,
            body: message
          });

content.title: Testing Argo CD and Flux Synchronization
content.explanation: GitOps synchronization testing validates that changes in Git are correctly applied to the Kubernetes cluster. This involves testing the entire workflow: Git commit → GitOps tool detection → synchronization → cluster update. Key aspects to test include: sync operation success/failure handling, conflict resolution, automatic retry mechanisms, health status reporting, and notification systems. Testing should simulate various scenarios: successful syncs, sync failures (e.g., invalid manifests), partial syncs, manual sync overrides, and automated sync policies. Integration tests should verify that the GitOps tool correctly reconciles cluster state with Git state and reports accurate status.

content.caption: Argo CD Application Manifest with Testing Configuration
content.code:
# applications/production/app-of-apps.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: production-apps
  namespace: argocd
  labels:
    environment: production
    managed-by: argocd
    test-enabled: "true"
spec:
  project: default
  
  # Source: Git repository containing applications
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/company/gitops-configs.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: applications/production
    
    # Directory recurse for app-of-apps pattern
    directory:
      recurse: true
      include: "*.yaml"
  
  # Destination: Target cluster
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  
  # Sync policy with automated testing hooks
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true  # Automatically delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true  # Automatically correct drift
      allowEmpty: false
    
    syncOptions:
      - Validate=true  # Enable validation
      - CreateNamespace=true  # Create namespaces if missing
      - PruneLast=true  # Prune resources last
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true
    
    # Retry configuration for failed syncs
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff:
        duration: 5s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 3m
  
  # Ignore differences for certain fields (prevents unnecessary syncs)
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
      jqPathExpressions:
        - .spec.template.spec.containers[]?.image
  
  # Health checks configuration
  healthChecks:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: Service
      name: my-service
      namespace: production
      checkType: "httpGet"
      path: "/health"
      port: 8080
    - apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: Deployment
      name: my-deployment
      namespace: production
      checkType: "deployment"
  
  # Post-sync hooks for testing
  hooks:
    # Pre-sync hook: Run before synchronization
    - name: pre-sync-validation
      hookType: PreSync
      command: ["sh", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          echo "Running pre-sync validation..."
          # Run custom validation scripts
          /scripts/validate-manifests.sh
          /scripts/security-scan.sh
          
          # Check cluster connectivity
          kubectl cluster-info
          
          echo "Pre-sync validation complete"
    
    # Post-sync hook: Run after successful synchronization
    - name: post-sync-tests
      hookType: PostSync
      command: ["sh", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          echo "Running post-sync tests..."
          
          # Wait for deployments to be ready
          kubectl wait --for=condition=available \
            --timeout=300s \
            deployment/my-deployment -n production
          
          # Run smoke tests
          /scripts/run-smoke-tests.sh
          
          # Verify service endpoints
          /scripts/verify-endpoints.sh
          
          # Send notification
          curl -X POST https://webhook.company.com/notify \
            -d '{"status": "success", "application": "production-apps"}'
          
          echo "Post-sync tests complete"
    
    # Sync-fail hook: Run when synchronization fails
    - name: sync-fail-handler
      hookType: SyncFail
      command: ["sh", "-c"]
      args:
        - |
          echo "Sync failed! Running recovery procedures..."
          
          # Send alert
          curl -X POST https://webhook.company.com/alerts \
            -d '{"alert": "sync-failed", "application": "production-apps"}'
          
          # Attempt automatic rollback if configured
          if [ "$AUTO_ROLLBACK" = "true" ]; then
            echo "Attempting automatic rollback..."
            /scripts/rollback-to-stable.sh
          fi
          
          # Log failure details
          kubectl get application production-apps -n argocd -o yaml > /tmp/failure-details.yaml
          
          echo "Sync failure handling complete"
  
  # Info for UI and notifications
  info:
    - name: description
      value: Production applications managed by Argo CD
    - name: maintainer
      value: platform-team@company.com
    - name: slack-channel
      value: "#production-deployments"
    - name: runbook
      value: "https://runbook.company.com/gitops/production"

---
# Sync status monitoring and alerting configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-notifications-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  service.slack: |
    token: $slack-token
  
  template.app-sync-status: |
    email:
      subject: Application {{.app.metadata.name}} sync status is {{.app.status.sync.status}}
      body: |
        {{if eq .app.status.sync.status "Synced"}}
        Application {{.app.metadata.name}} is successfully synced.
        {{else}}
        Application {{.app.metadata.name}} sync failed!
        Sync Status: {{.app.status.sync.status}}
        Health Status: {{.app.status.health.status}}
        Message: {{.app.status.operationState.message}}
        {{end}}
    
    slack:
      attachments: |
        [{
          "title": "Application {{.app.metadata.name}}",
          "title_link": "{{.context.argocdUrl}}/applications/{{.app.metadata.name}}",
          "color": "{{if eq .app.status.sync.status "Synced"}}good{{else}}danger{{end}}",
          "fields": [
            {
              "title": "Sync Status",
              "value": "{{.app.status.sync.status}}",
              "short": true
            },
            {
              "title": "Health Status",
              "value": "{{.app.status.health.status}}",
              "short": true
            }
          ]
        }]
  
  trigger.on-sync-status-unknown: |
    - description: Application synchonization has unknown status
      oncePer: app.metadata.name
      send:
        - app-sync-status
      when: app.status.sync.status == 'Unknown'
  
  trigger.on-sync-failed: |
    - description: Application synchronization failed
      oncePer: app.metadata.name
      send:
        - app-sync-status
      when: app.status.sync.status == 'Failed'
  
  trigger.on-deployed: |
    - description: Application is successfully synced and healthy
      oncePer: app.metadata.name
      send:
        - app-sync-status
      when: app.status.sync.status == 'Synced' and app.status.health.status == 'Healthy'

steps.title: Create Stable Baseline
steps.description: Establish a known-good deployment state in Git.
steps.details: Tag a specific Git commit as the stable baseline. Ensure this state is thoroughly tested and validated in staging.

steps.title: Simulate Bad Deployment
steps.description: Intentionally introduce a breaking change to Git.
steps.details: Create a PR with intentional errors: invalid manifest, broken configuration, or incompatible version change. Merge to trigger GitOps sync.

steps.title: Monitor Failure Detection
steps.description: Verify GitOps tools detect and report the failure.
steps.details: Check that Argo CD/Flux correctly identifies the sync failure, updates status, and sends alerts. Validate health checks fail appropriately.

steps.title: Execute Git Revert
steps.description: Use Git operations to revert to the stable baseline.
steps.details: Run 'git revert' or 'git reset' to return to the stable commit. Push changes to trigger automated sync back to known-good state.

steps.title: Verify Rollback Success
steps.description: Confirm cluster returns to stable state.
steps.details: Monitor GitOps synchronization. Verify applications return to working state. Run post-rollback validation tests.

steps.title: Test Automated Rollback
steps.description: Configure and test automated rollback triggers.
steps.details: Set up automated rollback based on health check failures or metrics thresholds. Test that automation works without manual intervention.

steps.details: Document steps for various failure types: configuration errors, resource constraints, network issues, dependency failures.

content.title: Canary Deployments and Progressive Delivery Testing
content.explanation: Advanced GitOps testing includes validating canary deployments, blue-green deployments, and other progressive delivery strategies. These patterns involve gradually rolling out changes to subsets of users while monitoring key metrics. Testing must validate that traffic splitting works correctly, metrics collection is accurate, rollback triggers function properly, and user experience remains consistent. Tools like Flagger or Argo Rollouts automate canary deployments in GitOps workflows. Testing scenarios include: canary initialization, progressive traffic shift, metrics analysis during rollout, automated rollback on failure, and promotion to stable. These tests ensure that progressive delivery mechanisms work reliably in production.

content.caption: Flagger Canary Deployment Configuration with Testing
content.code:
# canary/backend-canary.yaml
apiVersion: flagger.app/v1beta1
kind: Canary
metadata:
  name: backend-service
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: backend
    managed-by: gitops
    test-scenario: canary-rollout
test: true  # Enable automated testing

spec:
  # Target deployment to control
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: backend
  
  # Service configuration for traffic routing
  service:
    port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
    portName: http
    
    # Gateways for ingress (if using Istio/Linkerd)
    gateways:
      - public-gateway
    hosts:
      - backend.company.com
    
    # Traffic policy
    trafficPolicy:
      tls:
        mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL
  
  # Analysis configuration for automated testing
  analysis:
    interval: 1m  # Check metrics every minute
    threshold: 5  # Maximum number of failed checks before rollback
    maxWeight: 50  # Maximum traffic percentage to canary
    stepWeight: 10  # Traffic increase per step
    
    # Metrics to monitor during canary
    metrics:
      - name: request-success-rate
        interval: 1m
        thresholdRange:
          min: 99  # Minimum success rate percentage
        query: |
          sum(
            rate(
              istio_requests_total{
                destination_workload="{{ namespace }}-{{ target }}-canary",
                response_code!~"5.."
              }[1m]
            )
          ) / 
          sum(
            rate(
              istio_requests_total{
                destination_workload="{{ namespace }}-{{ target }}-canary"
              }[1m]
            )
          ) * 100
      
      - name: request-duration
        interval: 30s
        thresholdRange:
          max: 500  # Maximum p95 latency in milliseconds
        query: |
          histogram_quantile(
            0.95,
            sum(
              rate(
                istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{
                  destination_workload="{{ namespace }}-{{ target }}-canary"
                }[1m]
              )
            ) by (le)
          )
      
      - name: error-rate
        interval: 30s
        thresholdRange:
          max: 1  # Maximum error rate percentage
        query: |
          sum(
            rate(
              istio_requests_total{
                destination_workload="{{ namespace }}-{{ target }}-canary",
                response_code=~"5.."
              }[1m]
            )
          ) / 
          sum(
            rate(
              istio_requests_total{
                destination_workload="{{ namespace }}-{{ target }}-canary"
              }[1m]
            )
          ) * 100
    
    # Webhooks for custom validation
    webhooks:
      # Pre-rollout tests
      - name: pre-rollout-check
        type: pre-rollout
        url: http://flagger-loadtester.flagger-system/
        timeout: 30s
        metadata:
          type: "cmd"
          cmd: "curl -sf http://backend-canary.production/health && \
                echo 'Pre-rollout check passed'"
      
      # Traffic increasing tests
      - name: increase-traffic-check
        type: rollback
        url: http://flagger-loadtester.flagger-system/
        timeout: 5s
        metadata:
          type: "cmd"
          cmd: "curl -sf http://backend-canary.production/smoke-test"
      
      # Post-rollout tests
      - name: post-rollout-tests
        type: post-rollout
        url: http://flagger-loadtester.flagger-system/
        timeout: 1m
        metadata:
          type: "cmd"
          cmd: |
            # Run comprehensive test suite
            ./run-integration-tests.sh \
              --target http://backend-canary.production \
              --duration 30s \
              --concurrency 10
            
            # Verify business metrics
            ./verify-business-metrics.sh \
              --service backend \
              --window 5m
  
  # Canary progression with automated testing
  canaryAnalysis:
    # Initial phase: deploy canary with 0% traffic
    initialDelay: 30s  # Wait before starting analysis
    initialWeight: 0   # Start with 0% traffic to canary
    
    # Step 1: 10% traffic with validation
    steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause:
          duration: 2m  # Monitor at 10% traffic
        analysis:
          webhooks:
            - name: "10pct-validation"
              type: "confirm-traffic"
              url: "http://analytics-service/validate"
              metadata:
                expected-traffic: 10
      
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause:
          duration: 3m  # Monitor at 25% traffic
      
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause:
          duration: 5m  # Extended monitoring at 50% traffic
        analysis:
          # Run load tests at 50% traffic
          webhooks:
            - name: "load-test-50pct"
              type: "test"
              url: "http://load-test-service/run"
              metadata:
                duration: "2m"
                users: 100
                ramp-up: 30s
      
      - setWeight: 75
      - pause:
          duration: 2m
      
      - setWeight: 100
      - pause:
          duration: 10m  # Final monitoring before promotion
  
  # Rollback configuration
  rollback:
    enabled: true
    maxRetries: 3
    
    # Conditions for automatic rollback
    triggers:
      - type: "metrics"
        name: "request-success-rate"
        threshold: 95  # Rollback if success rate drops below 95%
      
      - type: "metrics"
        name: "request-duration"
        threshold: 1000  # Rollback if p95 latency exceeds 1000ms
      
      - type: "webhook"
        name: "custom-rollback-trigger"
        url: "http://monitoring-service/should-rollback"
  
  # Promotion configuration
  promotion:
    enabled: true
    
    # Conditions for automatic promotion
    conditions:
      - type: "metrics"
        name: "request-success-rate"
        threshold: 99  # Promote if success rate is above 99%
        duration: "5m"  # Must maintain for 5 minutes
      
      - type: "webhook"
        name: "business-metrics-check"
        url: "http://business-metrics-service/validate-promotion"
    
    # Actions after promotion
    actions:
      - type: "webhook"
        name: "notify-promotion"
        url: "http://notification-service/promotion-complete"
        metadata:
          channel: "#deployments"
          message: "Canary promotion completed for {{ .Metadata.Name }}"
      
      - type: "custom"
        name: "cleanup-old-versions"
        command: "kubectl delete deployment backend-v1"
